name: Rapoport's Rule
statement: Species near the poles tend to have wider ranges than those near the equator.
meaning: Rapoport's rule is the ecogeographical generalisation that the latitudinal extent of species' geographic ranges tends to be smaller at low latitudes, in the tropics, and larger toward the poles. Mean range size increases with latitude. It was proposed partly to help explain the latitudinal diversity gradient, the fact that far more species live in the tropics, but it is a contested pattern of limited generality.
mechanism: The leading proposed explanation is the climatic variability hypothesis. High-latitude species endure large seasonal and annual swings in climate, which select for broad climatic tolerances and, in turn, permit wide geographic ranges. Tropical species, living under relatively stable climates, evolve narrower tolerances and so occupy smaller ranges. If tropical species pack into narrow ranges, more of them can coexist, which was Rapoport's proposed link to the abundance of tropical diversity. Other explanations invoke the extinction of narrow-ranged species by past glaciations at high latitudes.

examples.text: Rapoport documented the pattern chiefly in subspecies of North American mammals, and Stevens drew on mammals and trees, the evidence from which the rule was first generalised.
For most groups that follow it, the pattern is distinct only above about forty to fifty degrees north, in the Palaearctic and Nearctic, rather than worldwide.
Marine teleost fishes show the greatest latitudinal ranges at low latitudes, the opposite of the rule: one of the clear cases where it fails or reverses.

variants.name: The climatic variability hypothesis
variants.text: The main proposed mechanism, that greater climatic variation at high latitudes selects for broad tolerances and hence wide ranges, one of several competing explanations.

variants.name: Extensions to elevation and depth
variants.text: Stevens's later applications of the same idea to altitude and to oceanic depth, extending the range-size gradient beyond latitude.

whyItMatters: It is a much-discussed proposed regularity in biogeography, tied to one of the great unsolved questions in ecology: why the tropics hold so many more species than higher latitudes. Even as its generality has been challenged, it has driven a great deal of work on how range size, climatic tolerance, and diversity vary across the globe, and on the pitfalls of measuring such patterns.

working.lead: Expect it mainly in the north
working.text: look for the range-size gradient chiefly in the Northern Hemisphere above about forty to fifty degrees, not as a global law.
keep the empirical pattern of range against latitude distinct from the climatic-tolerance mechanism proposed to explain it.
beware the method of averaging ranges over latitudinal bands, which can bias results, and prefer the midpoint approach.

limits: The rule is contested and not universal. For most groups it is distinct only above roughly forty to fifty degrees north, and it fails or reverses in the Southern Hemisphere, in the tropics, and in marine systems; Rohde concluded it is a largely local phenomenon. Gaston, Blackburn, and Spicer judged the evidence equivocal and the rule at best of limited generality. The original method of averaging the ranges of all species crossing each latitudinal band can bias results, and sampling artifacts can produce spurious patterns. Its causal link to the tropical diversity gradient is debated, and may be partly a statistical byproduct of it.
misreadings: It is a tendency with strong regional and taxonomic exceptions, not a universal law, and the evidence is concentrated in the Northern Hemisphere above about forty degrees. It does not definitively explain the tropical diversity gradient; that causal connection is disputed and may be partly a methodological artifact. And the climatic-variability mechanism is one of several competing hypotheses, not a confirmed cause: the pattern can exist without it holding.
origin: Named by George C. Stevens in a 1989 paper in The American Naturalist after Eduardo H. Rapoport, who had documented the pattern for North American mammal subspecies in his work Areography; its generality was sharply questioned by Gaston, Blackburn, and Spicer in 1998.

sources.text: Rapoport's rule, Wikipedia. — the range-size-increases-with-latitude statement, the climatic variability hypothesis, and the limits and reversals.

Stevens, "The Latitudinal Gradient in Geographical Range: How So Many Species Coexist in the Tropics," The American Naturalist 133(2):240-256 (1989). — the naming of the rule and its link to the diversity gradient.
Gaston, Blackburn & Spicer, "Rapoport's rule: time for an epitaph?" Trends in Ecology & Evolution 13(2):70-74 (1998). — the argument that the rule is of limited generality.
